title: Hulk
edition: Ang Lee’s US theatrical feature, 138 minutes, starring Eric Bana
synopsis: Bruce Banner survives a laboratory accident. As his body begins to change, the return of his father brings a buried childhood memory to the surface.
verdictRationale: Bruce uses his strength to protect Betty and admits to her that losing control can feel good. That admission gives families a way to discuss anger honestly. The film also invites viewers to enjoy the destruction Bruce fears in himself.
ageRationale: The flashback to a child threatened by his father may trouble viewers long after the monster fights. The frightening dog attack and repeated transformations also weigh in favor of waiting until the teen years.
reflection: Bruce can tell Betty something painful about himself because she listens. In an Orthodox examination of conscience, his admission suggests a harder question than who started a fight: what part of getting even did I enjoy?

themeScripture.text: Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
themeScripture.connection: Paul asks what good we can do when someone has wronged us. Bruce cannot undo what his father did to him, but he can keep Betty from paying for it. Where might he find help when there is no one left to fight?

title: Elektra
edition: Rob Bowman's original 2005 US theatrical release, 97 minutes (AFI)
synopsis: A contract killer discovers that her next targets are Mark and his daughter Abby. Refusing the assignment puts her between the family and another band of assassins.
verdictRationale: Elektra risks her life for the people she was paid to kill. That choice gives the story moral weight. Its opening also treats her skill at killing hired guards as a spectacle, and much of her work as a protector still consists of disposing of enemies.
ageRationale: An opening assassination leaves blood on a blade. A later beheading is implied, and a child is targeted by supernatural attackers. These scenes and repeated profanity weigh in favor of older teens.
reflection: Stick asks whether protecting Abby is Elektra’s way of paying for her sins. An Orthodox family might ask what repentance asks of her after the danger passes. Abby needs an adult she can trust even when there is no enemy to fight.
